utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, please. Call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I hear and I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Appearances, Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you too. Good morning to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Same procedure as yesterday. We start with your solemn declaration once more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down and Ms. Korner will be continuing with your cross-examination. May I have an indication as to what is going to happen today?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that I think it's examination-in-chief, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's like as always. When everyone is dealing with documents, one tends to underestimate. I will undoubtedly I think finish today. No question about that. Whether I finish, if Your Honour is only going to sit until 1.00 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can potentially I can sit until the very end, quarter to 2.00, because I only need to be at the airport at 3.00 even half past 3.00 I might be getting a lift here and if that leaves earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I think having looked at the remaining documents, plus there are a couple of videos, more than a couple, but I'm not going to play all of them, some of them are very lengthy. I think realistically I'll finish today, but it may not be there is much time to start cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only very quickly because I do want to get on. The only problem that arises is this: Despite my best efforts Judge Schomburg is sitting, I think, well at different times at different days next week but the main problem is going to come on Tuesday, where Judge Schomburg has asked -- the judges themselves are calling a witness who I'm due to cross-examine and Mr. Koumjian is due to come back to this Court to call a witness. It's all got itself into a terribly complicated state. All I need to know really is: Is Mr. Ackerman likely to finish in one full session, i.e., on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's very difficult tore me to say, Your Honour. I would say it's unlikely but possible. That's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will just have to see how we can go then. I don't know how we are going to sort Tuesday out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do let me know if there is a problem so that perhaps I could add myself thinking together with you and try and find a solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or put some pressure elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's an all day sitting on Tuesday, I know, and although I did express to Judge Schomburg that there were going to be problems because we were still on the Prijedor section, I think he's very anxious to get a move on and indeed, I think our concerns were also echoed by the Defence but didn't achieve very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's start and then we'll see how we get along.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm still, Colonel Selak, going to deal with the newspaper articles with respect to what was being said and other documents about the presence of non-Serb officers in the military. We dealt yesterday with the article of the 27th of March. Could you now be shown please an article of the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is Izetbegovic declared war, thank you, which will become Exhibit P1581.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, an article in the Glas newspaper. It starts -- it dealt with a press conference that was being given by the SDS regional board, and it's the vice-president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina speaks. Then Banja Luka, this is apparently quoting Mr. Brdjanin, "It was very quiet in Banja Luka last night which was indeed our goal, to stall Alija Izetbegovic for at least two days since the Serbian Defence forces had foreseen what was being prepared. Radoslav Brdjanin, vice-president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and member of the crisis detail, told journalists today." Pausing there for one moment. I think we discussed the arrival of the SOS so-called in Banja Luka at around this time, and were you aware, when you read this article, that they had demanded that a Crisis Staff be set up?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that, and when I read that in the paper, I was shocked. I was an active officer and this was something that really amazed me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because until that time, I was convinced that a solution would be found by peaceful means, that we would stay in one army, that there won't be an escalation. And they promised that things would calm down, that war would be avoided and it wouldn't be like it was in the Croatian part so that this threat surprised me. Not only myself but all officers, Muslim and Croat ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right you're speaking about what comes later then. So let's just look at it. Brdjanin went on, I'll leave out the Bosanska Krajina bit. "In addition, Brdjanin stated that the crisis committee is resolute in its implementation of all the demands that have so far been designed upon. All the changes in personnel will be decided upon by April the 15th." And he proposed that meetings were held. And then he talked about people working in the post office, the bank, he described Alija Izetbegovic declaring war on the Serbian people. And then Dr. Vukic spoke. And then Brdjanin went on to talk about Koljevic and Djeric, a man named Cizmovic, and Brdjanin remarked that it was precisely the composition of the crisis committee, headed by Predrag Radic that showed who the Serbian Defence forces believe in and whom they trust. And the journalist dealt with -- then mobilisation was talked about. And then this, "There are some negative elements in the army itself, like those who will artificially foment such disorder and that is why I am ordering Osman Selak, Vinko Radman, Mesud Hasotic, and Ludvik Kranjc to go ahead and pack their bags and go back to their homes, Dr. Vukic stressed. We support Major general Momir Talic, but if the above-mentioned persons do not withdraw of their own will, the Serbian defence forces will do it for them, Vukic concluded." Did you take those words when you read them, Colonel Selak, as seriously-meant words?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did take those words seriously, but I still lived in the hope that this problem would be positively resolved, that we would not have major problems. However, other officers, Muslims and Croats, took that even more seriously and they came out in favour of the federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I remained in my function and I believed, as long as I needed the army or as long as I performed my tasks conscientiously, I would not have any problems so I remained until the 19th of May when I submitted my application for retirement. There were threats by telephone, some disturbances, but I understood that they were individuals who were prompted by this very article. So they were the ones who made those telephone threats. So I didn't pay any attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This orders you to go ahead, pack your bags, and go back to your home, where was your home, Colonel Selak?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an apartment from the army in Banja Luka, and I stayed there until 1995. I couldn't leave Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Now, I would like you to look at a record of a speech made by Mr. Brdjanin in the assembly that was held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May. That's Exhibit P50 and it's at page 28 of that exhibit, in the translation, and if I'm given the B/C/S, I can find the B/C/S. In fact, I think it would help -- we've separated --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've separated so I can actually give the witness my copy of the B/C/S. And could we put the English up on the ELMO? In the B/C/S, it's at -- from there onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the ERN number, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of the English translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's page 28 with the ERN number is 01908538.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you fine the part, please, Colonel Selak, it's a sentence that begins, "The problem for areas where the Serbs are a majority is this:" And it's the bottom of our page 28.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 20 and 19 in my copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, 28 for us. For you, if you just go down the speech, I should think it's still on page 20 somewhere, and if anybody from the Defence team can assist to speed matters up as to where he'll find it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the document but my page 28 is a speech by Vojo Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you'd go for the ERN number of the translation, 01908538.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't help that. But you want page 01908538 in English, but I would welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've apparently given me a different version of that document than you have. The 16th session of the assembly held on 12th May, 1992, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is the 12th of May, Banja Luka, if you look wherever it is, Mr. Ackerman, I'm not concerned where you've got to. I would like the witness to find the part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I would like to find it too, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then you have a look for it. Brdjanin comes after -- try your page 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, Brdjanin begins speaking there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. If you go to page 30 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak have you now found the part, the sentence that begins, "The problem for areas where the Serbs are a majority"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found that sentence, which begins, "The problem of areas where the Serbs are in a majority is as follows."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. If you just follow then while I deal with it. Is this that, "Most of them are still asking whether they should injury the Muslims, whether they can hold certain posts, whether loyal Muslims and loyal Croats exist. When I spoke with General Raseta six months ago, when he asked me how many Croats hated the army, I retorted 100 per cent."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I don't know whether it was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. misread or what's going on. Ms. Korner is reading and she says, "Most of them are still asking whether they should injury the Muslims. I think what she says -- now, what I have says: The problem facing the areas where the Serbs are the majority is this: That most of them are still thinking they should not offend the Muslims. Nothing in there about injuring the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, we have got two translations. Your Honour, there are two. This has been translated twice. I will stick to the one that Mr. Ackerman -- I don't know what Your Honours -- which ones Your Honours have got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have it. We've checked thoroughly even on the list of the documents that were handed to us. We don't have this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honour looks at the second page, you'll see speech by Brdjanin, 12th of May assembly, Exhibit P50. It's five from the bottom of page 2 of the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but we do have it written there but we don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Korner, and please for fairness' sake, use the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to use the same translation that -- that -- where are we? I know that. I understand that. I just want it back on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My 20 is different.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's on page 30 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am sorry about this, Colonel. Can we go back I'll read this sentence again as it's in this translation." When I spoke with General Raseta six months ago when he asked me how many Croats hated the army, I retorted 100 per cent. That is not true, he says, and I say 101 per cent." Firstly, who was General Raseta?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Raseta was part of the 5th army district in Zagreb. He was the deputy commander. Later when the army command withdrew from Zagreb, he remained in that area and he conducted negotiations with the Croatian forces about pulling out the units of the JNA from Croatia. He attended meetings in Banja Luka with General Uzelac. I was present at those meetings and they discussed precisely how to pull out the units from Croatia that remained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just tell us what ethnicity was that general.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then Brdjanin went on to talk about the campaign, and I don't think we need trouble by that. He then talked about General Kukanjac insisting that the Court be moved from Banja Luka to Sarajevo, and at the end of that paragraph, said this, "Now, whoever was responsible for this" and that's talking about the hospital in Ljubljana should be put into the front ranks to go and bomb this hospital. I cannot fathom that we have still not learned some sense. To argue this, I will use the following facts: How can anyone still believe it is all right that we have a Muslim teaching political classes in the Banja Luka Corps?" Pausing there, to whom was he referring?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, he's thinking about Colonel Colonel Mesud Hasotic, who also received threats via newspapers that he had to leave the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then he went on to say, "I do not think it is. I know that people will not like what I am saying here, but I truly believe in what I say. I am less of a chauvinist than many believe. I merely have a high degree of national awareness and I believe that in conditions of war, once it is proclaimed, the entire economy, all war planning, all guarding of the facilities, must be put into the hands of Serbs. But once we are liberated, once we have established our own state, we will have nothing against employing experts of the other nationality. Let us not delude ourselves any more with empty talk about how we shall arrange this or maybe this will happen. I have also proposed that we give most of the leading positions to people from the areas where Serbs are the minority. They know what the mujahedin are and what the Ustashas are." And then he goes on to talk about the various areas. Now, did you -- it appears this assembly was televised. Did you see the meeting on the 12th of May on television?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you told about the speech that Brdjanin had made?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This speech was reported in the daily newspapers, in the media, it was broadcast over Radio Banja Luka several times. So people in town commented on this discussion and they took it very seriously, and as a threatening one. It is precisely statements like this which led to the removal of all officials, Muslims and Croats, in various institutions in the region of Bosnia-Herzegovina from schools, from different economic facilities and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think, as we'll see, it also had an affect on the army. Can we look now, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have I made that exhibit? I don't think I have. It's already P50.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at P229, which comes from the Sanski Most documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to have you basically strike from the record 11, line 21, where Ms. Korner says: "As we'll see, it also had an effect on the army." That's nothing but her testimony or submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm anticipating the evidence. But, Your Honour, there is no such thing as strike from the record. The record exists. I've never understood what happens in the United States about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think they have it the same way we do it here. But in any case, point taken, Mr. Ackerman, and I think Ms. Korner agrees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree. And I'll just deal with the documents when I get to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This P50 remains P50, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P229, please. Could we have the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And could you at some point in time, Ms. Korner, please, replace it with -- because the one we have is the one you were reading initially with the part, "should injure the Muslims." So if you have the other text, we would rather have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the official exhibit, though, Your Honour, contains the text that Mr. Ackerman is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So somehow or other, you and I managed to get another translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no big deal, because I have at least annotated on mine that there is a divergence between this and the other translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. This other document is 229?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P229, Your Honour, in the Sanski Most exhibits. It's a document dated the 7th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, I don't imagine that you saw this one at the time. You've seen it since; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see it before. I saw it after the war. I have one copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this was a meeting of political representatives of the municipalities of Bihac, Petrovac, Srpska Krupa, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Kljuc. And it was sent to the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka and the leadership of the Serbian Republic, and the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. Paragraph 1, which I will summarise, says it's necessary to declare a state of war. 2: They want a clear position from the highest authorities in respect of forging a land corridor. 3: Within the next three days, we request clear answers from the political leadership of the SDS and the military leadership of the Republic of -- Serbian Republic, on the question of reorganisation of the former JNA, now the VRS. We request to see the law on the army of the Serbian Republic. And 4: We demand that the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka, and particularly General Momir Talic of the 1st Krajina Corps, purge the 1st Krajina Corps of Muslims and Croats. We believe that they cannot fight against their own people and that they are now involved in intelligence and other activities in the 1st Krajina Corps that are of interest to Ustasha forces and members of the so-called Alija's Territorial Defence. Deadline for completion, seven days. 5 deals with definition of borders, which they found necessary from the military point of view. And 6: "All seven municipalities in our subregion agree that Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities until a level is reached where the Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented on its own territory in each of these municipalities. In this respect, we request the Crisis Staff provide a corridor for the resettlement of Muslims and Croats to central Bosnia and Alija's independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because they voted for it. If the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in Banja Luka fails to solve this issue, our seven municipalities will take all Muslims and Croats under military escort from our municipalities to the centre of Banja Luka." Now, you didn't see this document at the time, although you saw it later. However, were you made aware that there had been this demand from leaders or political representatives of these municipalities at any stage?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that this document existed. I found out about it after the war. However, already in the month of June, officers who were Croats and Muslims, or rather Bosniaks, had left their units, were dismissed from duty, and were sent to the federal Republic of Yugoslavia to resolve status matters there. At the same time, Muslims and Croats started moving out of Bosanska Krajina, especially from Banja Luka, in the direction of Croatia. That went on all the way up to the 18th of May, 1995, for as long as I was in Banja Luka, but it continued afterwards as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want you next, please, to have a look at a document dated the 9th of June, and it's 4.636. All right. Now, this is a document sent, apparently, by Colonel Vukelic whom we have mentioned before, the assistant commander for moral guidance, to the main staff, and it's dated the 9th of June and the importance of the number we'll see. But it's 488-3, and it says: "Report on the autonomous region Crisis Staff decision submitted to the main staff. One of the issues that was discussed at yesterday's session of the ARK Crisis Staff was the general personnel policy in the army 1st Krajina Corps. It was stated that within units of the 1st Krajina Corps, logistic base, and the units of the air force and anti-aircraft defence in Banja Luka garrison, there are 67 officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality. An ultimatum was issued requesting removal of these persons from vital and command posts by the 15th of June, 1992, or they will take over the control of -- over the armed forces. We consider their demand to be justified. But it is impossible to find adequate professional replacements among the reserve staff and active officers of Bosnia-Herzegovinian origin are not arriving from the FRY. Such action would also significantly weaken the above-named units from which it has been requested that staff be purged. We are aware of a certain degree of danger, and we are excluding such persons from the important decision-making processes. Our recommendation is to accelerate the process of sending active soldiers of Bosnian origin over from the FRY. The 1st Krajina Corps command should make the decision as to which staff members from the ranks of Muslims and Croats may still be temporarily kept and at what posts. It would also be essential to take a position on what should be done with those who have not demonstrated any hostile activity so far but who must be removed from key posts." And that's signed. Now, can you look a look, please, at the response to this, 4.1061? That documents will become -- I'm sorry, the one of the 9th of June, 1582 or the one we just looked at. This is dated the same day. It's from the main staff, addressed to a Colonel Rankovic. Who was Colonel Rankovic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Rankovic was head of the personnel department at the corps command in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Addressed to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and refers to the document giving the number of the previous document that we just looked at. "Officers of Muslims or Croatian nationality must be sent on leave immediately. Take action at once to refer them to the army of the FRY in order to resolve their status in the service." Did you ever see these two orders?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay in Banja Luka, I never saw these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, what effect did this order from the main staff to the 5th or 1st corps as it was by then of the Krajina Corps have? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely in the month of June, all officers who were Croats and Bosniaks were dismissed from their positions. Only two or three Bosniaks remained. Two of them changed their names. They took Serb names. And they remained there until the end of the war. These are non-commissioned officers. However, as for my own officers, Muslims and Croats, in the month of June, I sent them by aircraft to Belgrade where they resolved their status. However, within a short period of time, they had to leave Yugoslavia and they went to Europe, to Western Europe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will become Exhibit P1583.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Ms. Korner, if it's okay with you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, just out of curiosity because it looks strange to me, having gone through several military documents and dispatches, this one seems, and the stamp seems to be just a date against the entry processed, which is 11 days after supposedly it was issued. Does that make sense to you? Could you provide us with some kind of explanation. If you look at the previous document, you'll see that it is dated 9 June, it was transmitted and received, and processed on the 9th June. This one doesn't show it was received. It shows it has been processed which possibly presumes that it has been received, but it shows it has been processed 11 days later. Do you think there is a reason for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, which was sent to the command of the forcers of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this document was sent by telefax. The difference is in 15 minutes' time. They received it at the communication centre and then dispatched it to the main staff. At the main staff, they received this document straight away. However, when they sent return information to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, they did not record the time when they received this document at the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Personally, I think it is not important because it was registered at the main staff and they did respond to this document, and it was faxed. And that can be seen by the time that is shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I just want to check something on -- sorry, Your Honour, my attention has been drawn to something but I need to have that checked before I can deal with it. Yes, now, Your Honour, there is one further document on this I want to deal with but first of all --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, on the first day you testified, you explained about the relationship that existed between the political bodies and the military, and you said that the political authorities set the objectives and tasks that were to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that the military then, through its own methods, carried out those tasks. How does what we've just looked at fit into that scheme?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just as I said, on the first day, there were joint objectives of the political and military leaderships. The only difference was regarding the methods of attaining that goal. The political authorities were carrying out ethnic cleansing through the police and other authorities, and the military resolved other military problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But that's a slightly different -- here what we've seen is political, either speeches or things said at press conferences by the politicians. What effect was this having on the army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had a major effect, because people from these areas came into the army. The families of the army members lived in that area. So it was very important what the political leadership thought, and what their objectives were. There were contacts on a daily basis. There were exchanges of information and views were accommodated between the political and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Thank you. Can we look then finally at one further document, same month and it's dated the 21st of June. It's from the 30th Partisan Brigade. I'm sorry, I have the gone, it's got number 00437725. It's disclosure 4.2166. It's headed "command of the 30th Partisan Brigade, strictly confidential," date 21st of June, and it's addressed to the command of the 1st Partisan Brigade. One of the last documents on our list. So the documents were organised in order of the list. It should be down there. Look, can we just --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 6 -- 5 and 6, Your Honour, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it doesn't have a disclosure number in our case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's why -- there was a disclosure number but -- Your Honour, I'm going to put up the English and here is this for the officer. I can't stand waiting much longer. And I'll put up the -- an English copy on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is -- it's headed, I think, Colonel Selak, "Answers to questions forwarded. The main staff of the army have forwarded to us the strictly confidential document of the 20th of June with the following content. In response to the questions raised by some units about the military service of soldiers of non-Serbian nationality in the army of the Serbian Republic, we are forwarding the following explanation: Soldiers of non-Serbian nationality are to be released from your units at their own request by applying one of the procedures set forth below. A: The units is to register" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the word "soldiers" has been missed out of the translation. We checked that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "To register the soldiers with the Red Cross as a prisoner so that he can be exchanged later for prisoners of the opposing side via this humanitarian organisation. Released soldiers are to travel to Belgrade and then be transferred home," et cetera. "And the soldiers are to be interviewed on what solution is most suitable for them. Soldiers of non-Serb nationality who wish to serve in the army of the Serbian Republic are to be kept in the units on less important duties and put under the necessary supervision. They should submit and personally sign a written statement." And then it deals further with soldiers of Serbian nationality. Now, Colonel, again, were you aware of this device that was to be adopted at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of such documents. I had them at the base command. Until the 18th of May, when the Army of Republika Srpska was proclaimed, soldiers who were doing their military service in the territory of Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia, and who originally came from Bosnia-Herzegovina, were born there, were supposed to return to their places of residence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Also, soldiers from Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia, who did their military service in the JNA units in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were supposed to be returned to their places of birth in Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia. This document clearly shows that. It was signed by the deputy commander of the 1st Partisan division, and the deputy commander signed this, but the commander was Colonel Galic. And that is precisely the type of action that was taken in all units of the 5th Corps, as well as in other units that were not within the corps. That is to say the logistics base, the rocket brigade, the school centre for training tank operators, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By the time that you actually left the army, which was the beginning -- you handed over your duties the beginning of July, how many non-Serb officers were still serving in the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any precise information, but I know that Colonel Hasotic, Mesud, stayed until the end of August, as well as Colonel Kranjc who towards the end of July, beginning of August, left his post and went to Slovenia. A few NCOs remained who changed their names into Serb names and they remained in their posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can we just finally on this topic go back for a moment to the document that you looked at earlier? Because there is one thing I missed out. It's the report by Colonel Vukelic, which is now Exhibit P1582. I said it was sent to the army main staff but what I think we -- I missed certainly, it was also sent to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you -- were you surprised that something like this should go both to the main staff of the army and the political -- the heads of the political wings of government?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, the assistant commander for morale and political and legal affairs, Colonel Milutin Vukelic, informs the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the decision of the Crisis Staff decision of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. That is to say this was a decision passed by the then authorities in Krajina concerning their demands or requests. This information is sent on behalf of the corps command, and I find this logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The question -- so the question was: Are you surprised to see it went not only to the main command of the army but also to, as it were, the head of the state?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That does not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's something you would have expected in respect of this kind of issue?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question here is very important. It pertains to the survival, to the life of a people in an area, and according to my opinion, this type of information is something that is expected. It's not something that surprised me. Members of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina regularly visited the corps command and toured the units at the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Then that's all I ask on this particular issue of the dismissals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour the last Exhibit that he read, the Partisan Brigade, will be Exhibit P1584.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I'd like to go back to your official notebook, please. You've got that in front of you. And we stopped there yesterday with the entry for the 28th of April, and now can we move, please, to the following day, the 29th of April, which is at our page 122, Your Honour. What were you reporting there, in that entry? It begins, "The Presidency of the SFRY on the 28th of April".

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information that the Presidency of the SFRY on the 28th of April had a meeting in its broader composition, attended by the President of the SFRY, the deputy Prime Minister, the vice-president of the assembly, the acting secretary for National Defence, and the deputy of the federal minister for foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I'm sorry, I know you received it but are you just recording that there was such a meeting or did somebody actually tell you about it? I mean, in other words, was there a meeting at your command at which you were being informed about the meeting of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was at a meeting with the commander of the 5th Corps when they all received this information, all of his deputies, and I was also present. So I noted down this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, the only thing I want to ask you about here is under 1, "International and internal situation, four republics would be a real Yugoslavia." And then you've written "not for a new Serbian state."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was that referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I just copied the information announced to us by the commander of the 5th Corps. Item 1, when he talks about the international and domestic situation, he said that Yugoslavia would comprise four republics, and those would be Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he said that he was not only in favour of a Serbian state, meaning that he would be in favour of it including Montenegrins, Macedonians, Bosnians and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what General Talic was saying on the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move, please, to the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item number 1, "Taking on conscripts and reserve officers, responding to the general mobilisation announced in the autonomous region." What kind of a meeting was this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment. I wrote this down for my own needs, for my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. command. This was about the induction of military conscripts. So conscripts and reserve members who were being called up at the request of Bosanska Krajina. At that moment, I was focusing on the problems that could arise from this whole matter, because the mobilisation was declared so we would need time to equip all these soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, item 5, there was a discussion with a Major Malic about command and control issues and threats to his life, which have been coming from men serving in his battalion. All I want to know is what ethnicity was Major Malic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Ivica Malic was a Croat and he was a commander of the medical [as interpreted] battalion in the rear base that was under my command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correct, the quarter master battalion.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Malic had to leave his duty urgently, and I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, finally, and only because we can see, I don't think it's of any interest, something is written I think across your page. You needn't bother to read it but I just want to know why it's written there.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a pen -- pencil, at a meeting of the commanders of the corps, they were requesting weapons from me. I was trying to stick to the law and to the regulations pertaining to the issuance of weapons. A man who was sitting to my left took a pencil and he wrote down, may I state this? May I read what it says here as it is written?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry, I don't think we need it, but it wasn't written by you. Somebody else wrote this in your book?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was written by -- it says, "Issue the equipment. Don't --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I know. Don't worry, we've got it. All right. Can we move, please, in your notebook to the 7th of May? There is an item written under 3, "The matter of Croat and Muslim personnel at the logistics base." What was that referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the question and answer regarding the previous documents. Croats and Muslims had to leave their posts. They were interviewed about where they wanted to go, whether they wanted to go to the federal Republic of Yugoslavia or abroad, and this was something that was reviewed at the level of their commands, this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just deal with one slightly subsidiary issue to this question of these dismissals? Did first of all serving officers receive accommodation from the army whilst serving with the army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The army bought apartments and awarded them to active officers as well as to civilians who were employed in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If an officer was forced to leave the army or forced to take early retirement, was he allowed to keep that accommodation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he remained in Banja Luka, yes, he would keep the apartment, and then later, he could buy it from the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, if he had to leave Banja Luka, would he be entitled to sell that accommodation or receive any compensation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't have the right to sell it or receive any compensation. Apartments were just left. The family would leave them with a suitcase. They would leave everything, their things, cars, garages, if people had them. Everything was left as it was, and this was taken by the military authorities and given to other officers, those who had arrived from Yugoslavia or Croatia or Slovenia, with the corps units. The proceedings are being conducted now to give back, to restore, those apartments to their prior occupants, and this process has not been completed yet. It's ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally on this, were there strictly defined offences under military law for which people could be dismissed from the army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You needn't bother to tell us what they are, but was there any offence which would allow for dismissal, forcing into early retirement, of simply being a Muslim or a Croat or a non-Serb generally?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the question of Muslim and Croat officers was being resolved, the factor was considered whether people who met the conditions for retirement could retire. However, all those who did not meet those conditions for retirement could go to the Republic of Yugoslavia or somewhere else. If anybody was criminally responsible, then this was something that was reviewed by Yugoslav courts and they would then make a ruling about that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Can we then move, please, in your official notebook, please, to -- it's an entry for the 11th of May, and it's under the heading, "Security." It's our page 130. "Security situation in Donji Vakuf. The town is empty. All residents gone. A ghost town." Did you see that yourself or was that a report to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment. I'm looking for that passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two under the 11th, two entries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What you should have is the quarter master -- it comes as "operations and training," and then "security".

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see the entry now, "Security situation in Donji Vakuf, the town is empty. All residents gone. A ghost town"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 11th of May? Just one moment. Yes, yes. I've found it. Security.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to know. Was that something you saw yourself or was that reported to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the depot in Donji Vakuf, Savic, told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we look, please, at another document outside of your diary, to follow things through in date order? It is another 30th Partisan Division document dated the 16th of May, 1992. Its number is 00437738, disclosure 4.1576. And it was three up from the bottom of our list. Now, this is again the 30th Partisan Division to the 1st Partisan Brigade, signed by Colonel Galic, and it's to do with protection of command posts and communication centres. It states, "After the takeover of communications centres and other separate communication facilities, communication links between the Ministry of the interior and the rump Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina have been blocked and disconnected." Can we pause there, please? Is what is being discussed here the MUP and what's described as the rump Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it were, the -- not sure how to put this exactly, it's not the real Bosnia-Herzegovina but it was the non-Serbian state institutions? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Consequently, communication is no longer possible and mail, telephone and telegraph messages, as well as radio and television signals cannot be transmitted." Were you aware of the takeover of --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- for example, the Kozara transmitter?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then what is said here, "The enemy will try to regain as many of these facilities as possible, as he tried with the attack on the Vlasic centre, in order to protect all these communication centres, eliminate the surprise factor, and secure communication -- all communication links between the units," and then there is -- there are a series of orders.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just so that we understand, in May of 1992, was there, as is stated in this document, was it almost impossible to communicate with the authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that be made P1585?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now can we move back to your official notebook, to the 18th of May --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there is not much left that I want to go through but this entry is a major one but I think it probably is better to break at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, needless to say, one should never have a break because I then do a check and I found that I had skipped one document on dismissals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. It's not the first time. It has happened to anyone, and it certainly won't be the last time. I just wanted to inform you that I have just signed the decision on rule 92 bis relating to Bosanski Novi municipality, minus of course as far as concerns witness 7.147 because we don't have the statement as yet. When we receive that, we will decide it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness be shown one last document on the question of, as it were, dismissals? It's disclosure number 4.594, 5th Corps command, dated the 15th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, this appears to be a draft or at least it's not signed, but it's Lieutenant commander -- I'm sorry, Lieutenant General Vladimir Vukovic. So that was -- General Vukovic was still in charge of the 5th Corps at that stage, presumably?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And all I want to deal with is the first paragraphs. "In regard to the coming retirement of a portion of the active military personnel, and the change of classification of some units of the 5th Corps, we would suggest the following changes in the personnel. 1: That Colonel Tepsic be appointed the head of the operative group, federal secretariat for people's Defence, for coordination with the logistics service of the UN forces. We would point out that according to an order issued by the federal secretariat, Colonel Osman Selak, current commander of the logistics base was in line for this post. We consider that at this moment this would not be an appropriate appointment." Did you see that order yourself?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of this order. At that time, I was already appointed by the chief of general staff of the Yugoslav People's Army as head of group for cooperation with the United Nations. I knew that Colonel Tepsic was nominated for that position. This was at the intervention of the corps commander but this was not taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- may that be made 1586?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, could we go back to your notebook entry for the 18th of May? Was this a meeting with General Talic and commanders of units within the corps, but the corps command staff only?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders of units were there in Banja Luka. The commander of the Armoured Brigade, the Rocket Brigade, I don't know who else was there, and also the top echelons of the command, that is to say the assistant commanders of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you then record what General Talic told you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I quoted it here in my notebook. First, under A he informed us about the meeting of the Crisis Staff that he attended. And he said --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause. Were you aware or did you know whether or not before the 18th of May, General Talic had attended meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he attended meetings of the Crisis Staff, but as for the timing and the questions involved, I never expressed any interest or did he tell me about it. Either Talic went or one of his assistant commanders, Vukelic, Vujnovic, or even Colonel Bosko Kelecevic, his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how would -- you say he didn't -- he personally didn't say he'd been to a meeting of a Crisis Staff except clearly on this occasion, but how would you know that he was attending or that Colonels Vujnovic or Vukelic were attending?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they went as representatives, either individually or together. I don't know about that. But we had regular communications. We worked in the same building. Our offices were there, near each other. So of course we had a normal day to day communication about various matters, including political matters as well, because I was interested too in what was going on in Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If an officer left the army building where you were based, did he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have to leave behind information as to where he was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a person left the command building or the workplace generally speaking, he would have to tell his superior officer where he was going, and also his subordinates had to know where he was going so that the subordinate could find his superior in case he needed to ask him about something. This is a normal type of relationship that exists within a unit. One always had to know day and night where the commander was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say this just says the Crisis Staff. To which Crisis Staff was this a reference? Because we know that there were two in Banja Luka, the regional and a municipal.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is from the meeting of the Crisis Staff, the regional one, because the corps covered the entire region, not only the municipality of Banja Luka, and therefore there is no logic for it only to be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we now look at the information that he provided you with? He said that, "Today was the establishment of the army of the Serbian Republic, the VRS, to be officially proclaimed, that there would be a change in the insignia."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On their caps, yes. The three-coloured flag.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, "In the area of responsibility of the corps, everything would be subordinate to --"

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. That everything would be subordinated to the corps. That is to say the entire area of responsibility was subordinated to the command of the 5th Corps with regard to all matters. That is to say all human and material resources of that territory fall under the corps and are there to meet the needs of an armed struggle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then there was a request apparently at the meeting to have the corps, the area of the corps, expanded, the formation of light brigades, an air force, and then there was something about Kosmos?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Kosmos will change ownership?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This specifically involves the establishment of light brigades too, that the school centre of the mechanised and army -- armoured unit, that is to say the military academy and the secondary school for tank operators would remain in Banja Luka and that the repair and overhaul centre Kosmos, which carried out the general overhaul of radars and similar systems for the needs of the entire JNA should remain in Banja Luka, and that it should change its owner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Then under B, proclamation, there was the order to disarm paramilitary formations, all those which have no permits. Does it read, "As far as Bosanski Novi and Srbac"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then the situation on the territory. And then --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanski Kobas, that that is where plundering was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. I want to try and summarise this, please, Colonel. And then if we go down the list that he was telling you about, there was a demand to open up a corridor leading to war -- leading to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff is opting for negotiations instead of war but this has to be resolved?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "No military leaders, no paramilitary formations" and then --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- "Muslim response if they do not want to fight, let them go."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, could you look, please, at document P227, the gazette for -- which recorded that meeting of the 18th of May at the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the translation, Your Honour, it's item number 12, and if the usher gives it to me, I'll find the relevant part for the witness. It's page 00882909.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We saw what you recorded as General Talic had told you. We look down at item numbers 3 and 4, "Illegally obtained weapons will be taken away by members of the military and civilian police." Was that something that General Talic told you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember this. This was not written.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because you recorded -- all right. Let's read the next one. "All formations that are not in the army of the Serbian Republic of BH, all the Banja Luka security services centre, and are in the Autonomous Region of Krajina are to be considered paramilitary formations and must be disarmed." Was that what was said to you which you recorded as proclamation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I included information that there were no voyvodas, those were the leaders of these paramilitary formations, but also I said that there were in paramilitary formations. That was the item I did include. So there were no vojvodas or paramilitary formations, and I believe this is a quotation from item 4 of the conclusions of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then if we go, please, to the conclusion number 14.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, conclusion, it's in paragraph 14 of the same meeting, which reads, in the gazette, "For the time being the 5th Corps is to take over the Kosmos air force maintenance and production complex until the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina comes to a final decision." Is that what you were recording under your one-line note in respect of Kosmos?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I put Kosmos. I said that Kosmos would change its owner and remain in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Colonel. You can put that away, then. That can be taken from you. Could we now move, please, in your notebook, just to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all briefly the 24th of May where you had a meeting with assistants, page 146 for us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It looks like the problem of Captain Trako was discussed again. Is that right? If you just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. And he was obviously interviewed again?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we move, please, to what happened on the 27th of May, when you had a meeting with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, on the 27th of May, were you aware that there was an attack being planned on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So no one in the command had informed you that there was going to be an attack?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've recorded on the 27th of May, at a meeting with the corps commander, it says reporting. Was that you reporting to the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a meeting at the corps commander's. There was this daily reporting. I came from Banja Luka with Colonel Tepsic because the command post was at the correctional facility of Hrvatska Gradiska on the other side of the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was there then a report about what had happened in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The head of the leading team of the corps command for that day was Colonel Dragan Marcetic assistant corps commander for operations and teaching. This team received information about occurrences during the day in the units of the corps. And at the meeting at General Talic's, he reported on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, using your note, what General Marcetic said and what General Talic's reaction was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Marcetic reported that that day in Kozarac, 800 citizens were killed, that 1.200 were taken prisoner. At that moment, I understood this information. I realised that Dragan Marcetic had diminished the number of persons killed in Kozarac. At that moment, General Talic knew that I was the only Bosniak among the officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you stop there for a moment, please? How did you know when he said that 800 citizens were killed that he had diminished the number of persons killed in Kozarac? At that moment, on the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marcetic knew that I was a Bosniak. We were relatively close, too. And it is precisely due to my presence that he diminished the figures involved. And this was later proven to be true unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So at that stage, you thought the figure of 800 was less than had actually been killed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that if I understand your evidence, that it was being reduced because Colonel Marcetic knew that you were a Bosniak and didn't want to give you the full figure?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Continue. What was General Talic's reaction to this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Talic's spontaneous reaction was to look at me, to turn his head towards me. He realised that he had made a mistake. He turned to Colonel Marcetic and used the following words: "You mean that 80 persons were killed, lost their lives? That is the information that you're supposed to send to the general staff." I will never forget these words for as long as I live.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why do you, in your opinion, being present at this meeting, what was the reason for General Talic saying, "You mean 80"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a normal reaction on his part, because he knew that he was violating the rules of international law of war. And that somebody had to be held accountable for that. And somebody would have to bear the consequences of this genocide, and he in actual fact wanted to conceal, cover up, the crime committed and to misinform his superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, then, back at your note about what else was said? You've recorded Kozarac and 800 dead, 1.200 captured. The next entry you write --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That people were at the end of their -- had reached the end of their patience, that four soldiers were killed and 17 wounded, that they were going to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by bus, and that this bus was stopped --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause there, Colonel, please. Is this still in relation to Kozarac or was this a different --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Colonel Marcetic here is reporting to the corps commander about what was going on in the corps, and in the area, on that day, the 27th of May, 1992, because this was a report made at 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the note about the actual attack on Kozarac stops, does it, in Kozarac because of a roadblock, 800 dead, 1.200 captured?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are some other issues further on about what was going on in the corps, that there were extremists on both sides, that an escalation will not -- that it would not be possible to prevent an escalation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just stop.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the large expenditure of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop for a moment, please. I'm not so interested in this. Could you turn, please, to the part where you talk about the paramilitary formation for Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That, "The paramilitary formation from Manjaca should leave the training ground." I'm reading it as I wrote it down at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was a reason given for that at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was saying the paramilitary's formations from Manjaca? Was that Colonel Marcetic or General Talic who was saying that they should leave?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Talic ordered for them to leave the training ground; that was his order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, on this entry, "He is against the war option, 800 killed." Again, was that General Talic saying that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff asked for an analysis of the manpower of the 5th Corps, and that he wasn't for the war option, and again he mentioned the 800 killed. I didn't put down Kozarac but it's understood that it's Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, the Chief of Staff of the main staff wasn't there, was he? This was General Talic saying what the Chief of Staff wanted?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was stated by Colonel Bosko Kelecevic, I'm not sure but I think that was his position, because he wanted an analysis of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did in the catch what the witness said. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, he wanted an analysis of the food supplies of the manpower.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that but what you've written, isn't it, is, "Chief of Staff, main staff"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the Chief of Staff to the main staff -- are we talking about the main staff of the 5th Corps or are we talking about the main staff at republic level?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether the main -- the Chief of Staff of the main staff of Republika Srpska was there. So I think that it was Colonel Bosko Kelecevic the Chief of Staff. Maybe I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. But who said -- who was against the war option, as 800 had been killed? Who said that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was stated by General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you look, please, at a different document? It's attachment 5 to the statement of the 13th of July, 2000. And it's a document dated the 27th of May, 1992, from the 1st Krajina Corps. This is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps, 27th of May. It says, "Stari Gradiska." Was that where the forward command post was at that stage?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was your -- had your meeting with General Talic been at that forward command post?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a report to the corps commander, and I went to report about the logistics supplies with Colonel Tepsic and his deputy for the rear. And we were in Banja Luka at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this is the report, as it's headed, on the elimination of the Green Berets, in the wider area of Kozarac village. So this is not just, do we take it, a report on the village or town of Kozarac but the surrounding areas as well?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Indeed, we can see that they are listed below. "Concerning the destruction of the Green Berets in the wider area of Kozarac village, we submit the following report, that the armed conflict started on 25th of May, 1992, and ended on the 27th of May." Now, by the words "armed conflict" what would you, as an army officer, understand by it? And what would the superior command understand by that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: An armed conflict is thought to be the conflict between two armies or two opposing sides, or two enemy units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would that include, in army terminology, an isolated incident where a vehicle had been fired upon, or a patrol had been fired upon?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a formulation, a term here, armed conflict between warring units, not an incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Participating in the armed conflict on our side were components of the 343rd Motorised Brigade, an enlarged motorised battalion, supported by two 105-millimetre howitzer batteries and one M-84 tank squadron." Now, how many men would that mean? Roughly?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The motorised brigade had 2.500 people by establishment, and it was augmented by a motorised tank unit and also it had howitzers. So it was a very well-equipped, armed unit of 3.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The total strength of the Green Berets was 1.500 to 2.000 men, without heavy weapons. Now, from your knowledge of this area, were there 1.500 to 2.000 armed Muslims, which is what Green Berets, I think, is meant to relate to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In this area, there were no armed formations of the so-called Green Berets. People returned their weapons at the request of the Prijedor municipality authorities. However, a genocide occurred here, ethnic cleansing. Otherwise, how can you explain that only four soldiers from this brigade were killed? And on the other side, over 1.500 people were actually killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- I was going to come on to ask you about that. I'm sorry, I've just been passed a note, after the millimetre -- 105-millimetre howitzers batteries, could you read the original? What does the next bit say? And 1, M-84 what?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states here a tank platoon of M-84. So there are four tanks in a platoon, and they were part of the equipment of the Yugoslav army. At that time, one of the tanks was among the most modern in the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to know, is there a difference between a -- showing my military ignorance, is there a difference between a platoon and a squadron?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Three platoons -- three squads make up a platoon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Three platoons make up a squad, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you sure about that, interpreter? Okay. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid there has been a mistranslation there. Colonel Selak, then we see overall results, "The wider area of Kozarac village, Kozaraca, Trnopolje, Jakupovici, et cetera, has been entirely freed of Green Berets." And then this, "80 to 100 Green Berets were killed and about 1.500 captured. Part of the Green Berets, 100 to 200 persons, at large on Mount Kozarac. Our own casualties are five killed and 20 wounded." Now, you touched on that. If as it is alleged in this report, there were 1.500 to 2.000 Green Berets and you told us that how many men the 343rd Brigade had, would you expect the casualties to be as low as five killed and 20 wounded?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's absurd. No professional soldier, if he read this, would believe it, particularly if you know that 343rd Brigade was very well equipped and well trained. In 1992, it was used to the utmost in fighting in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then it's signed by Colonel Marcetic. So was this his official report to the 1st Krajina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report to the main staff of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was signed by the chief of the control team for that day, Colonel Marcetic, who had to make a report to the main staff. And the communication centre received it at 2100 hours and then sent it on at 22 hours 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that after the time of the meeting that you have described in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then attached to this document, is there a list of the 1st Krajina Corps's effective strength? Although I think it was a separate document.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because the dating and timing is -- and I don't think we need trouble to go through these figures at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that be made 1587, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you to look, please, at one more document and then your notebook for the 1st of June. Could you be shown, please, attachment 2 to that statement of the 13th of July, 2000?
