utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look at the document, thank you. Sorry, what's he been given? Thank you very much, Colonel Selak, can you hand back the previous document? This is dated the 1st of June, from the 1st Krajina Corps, addressed to the main staff, and it's a combat report, and it describes the situation in the units under item 2. The 1st Krajina Corps units in the area of -- areas of Prijedor, Sanski Most, Prijedor -- Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Jajce, in control of the situation and are continuing the mopping up of the terrain and the seizing of weapons from formation members." Now, what do you understand -- what is the meaning of the military use of the term "mopping up"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "mopping up" implies the clearing of terrain of enemy soldiers, of enemy units, the manpower of enemy units and I'm speaking now in the military sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does it have anything to do with physically pushing a brush around a floor or a piece of ground or something like that? The civilian use of a mop-up?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We are talking here about ethnic cleansing, the removal of people from that area. In the military sense, that is clear. Clearing the terrain of enemies, enemy peoples from that terrain, of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that's what happened here but I'm just -- I just want, in normal terms, if it wasn't for this situation, you say "ethnic cleansing." I just want to know, if it was used - not in the terms of this conflict - it would have meant simply clearing the terrain, would it, of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, if I may inform the Court, the Trial Chamber, about the previous document that I looked at, when I said that 343rd Brigade had 3.000 people, in the document that I had a minute ago, it states clearly, gives a list of the manpower of the units, and that brigade actually numbers 5.500 men. So I'm correcting myself. Not 3.000 but 5.500 people, and this is stated in a report by the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right, Colonel Selak, I whipped it away too quickly. That's right. All right. Now, can we look, please, at -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that be made P1588?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back to your notebook?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For the 1st of June, I think you had a number of meetings that day, did you? Because it starts -- or was this a meeting, all one meeting with the commander? Was it all one meeting with the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, General Talic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 1st of June, I had a meeting with my officers from the command, from my base, and after that, I made a report to the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just dealing with your meeting, first of all, you've recorded, have you, that on -- you were providing rations for 119.000, nearly 120.000 men?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you note that the 2nd Krajina Corps had approximately 22.000 men?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the correct number, 22.000, at that point that was the number of men in the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So if you were actually also providing rations at that stage, were you, for the 2nd Krajina Corps? Because if we look at a note, you say excluding the 2nd Krajina Corps, that's for ours, our benefit, over the page, 159, there were 78.780?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was Sipovo and Srbac and Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sipovo and Srbac had a brigade each numbering 1.800 men and the operative group of Doboj had 15.000 men, which makes about 100.000 people in the 1st Krajina Corps. The 2nd Krajina Corps had 20.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that's all I want to ask about your meeting with your corps. Did you then, however, have a meeting with the 1st Krajina Corps commander, General Talic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same day, in the afternoon, I had a meeting or I reported to the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've recorded there that there was a most difficult situation in the Bosnian Krajina, maybe in Banja Luka too. Muslims were dying because of Croats. This is the case in Prijedor. First, who is speaking? Whose remarks are those?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are General Talic's words.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did he mean -- or what did you understand him to mean when you recorded, "Muslims were dying because of Croats. This is the case in Prijedor"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that because Muslims had placed themselves on the side of the Croats. They were joining their army, and that is why they were getting killed. And what happened in Bosanska, Krajina, and Kozarac and broader happened precisely because of that, because the Muslims took the side of the Croats and that is why the corps did what it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then under assignments, "Arm all soldiers at Manjaca." And then you've recorded and you've ticked that. And under 4, prisoner of war camp at Manjaca urgent for approximately 2.500 people. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was -- in general terms, what was the discussion about Manjaca at that stage?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander, during the reporting, issued tasks, and I wrote down the word "assignments". Under 1, he ordered that all soldiers at Manjaca should be armed. The paramilitary formations that were being trained at Manjaca, each of those people in those forces were not personally issued with a weapon. They had tank firing training, training from rifles, machine-guns, cannon and so on. So this order states that soldiers should be issued with infantry weapons, rifles, semi-automatic rifles, individually, and they should also sign after each one receives an individual weapon, because during the training, they are not issued with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, under 4, where was the figure of 2.500 people coming from?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know where people were supposed to come from, but this provided scope for creating a camp for prisoners of war at Manjaca for approximately 2.500 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, again, could you now look in connection with that at a document which was attachment 1 to the statement of the 13th of July, 2000? Document dated -- appears to be dated 1993 but that's a typing error, I think. Can you just tell us, what is the date? I think what's happened is it's the photocopy is very bad.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 7th of June, 1992, when the camp for prisoners of war at Manjaca was opened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It does look as though it's 1993 when you get to the next -- but it's obviously an error, I think. On the basis of the order of the main staff, the 7th of June --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, that may be right, having put that in, I'm not sure that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, Ms. Korner, it seems that on the original, on the B/C/S, the year 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Doesn't appear once.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It appears twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It appears three times. It appears in the reference 353 something/93. Then it appears immediately beneath that, 07/06/1993. Then it appears again, three, four, lines, the first line of the first paragraph, second line. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'll ask the Colonel, but I need -- I think -- before I put this in, we know Colonel Popovic was appointed but I do know that the camp was then reopened again later. So I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Despite the fact it says 1993 and it seems to deal with members of the HVO --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think if I may I'll leave this and I need to do a check because I don't want to take a false point with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me just to say two words in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The camp for prisoners of war at Manjaca was closed down on the 15th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. But -- well, I'm sorry, perhaps, Colonel, you better tell us the answer. Have you seen this order? Because it does say 1993. Is this an order you've seen before or saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw this order before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, I think I'll leave it and check it and come back to. Thank you very much, perhaps after a break. Can we then, please, now -- I think in -- look at a meeting that in fact was on the 4th of June, 1992, at our page 167. Now, this is a meeting at the Banja Luka municipal assembly with the President of the Banja Luka municipal assembly and director-general of a particular company. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it seems to be dealing with Kosmos. Do you know how this meeting came about, why you attended a meeting at the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was commander of the logistics base and what Radi Cajevec did, as well as the Kosmos overhauling facility, I was the one who took over these commodities, these goods, and I put them in warehouses or rather sent them out to various units. So I was directly in charge of that, and I invited to this meeting precisely for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The introductory remarks were made by Mr. Radic, the president of the assembly. Did you also record, however, that Brdjanin was at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because you've recorded him as saying that the production of ammunition and so on and so forth must begin as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, this is a long time ago, and if you can't remember, please say so. Do you have any recollection now of this meeting, apart from your note?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that meeting. General Djukic attended and General Ninkovic. There was my second meeting at president Radic's. The first one was when I was head of the group for cooperation with the United Nations that had to do with facilities. And this was the second one I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think that's all I want to did you about that. Can we move, then, and there is only two more entries in your notebook that I want to look at -- before we do that because we are going to move to very shortly before you left the army. Could you look, please, at another document, which has already been produced? It's P256.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say I've been given some instructions that that document is 93, when the camp was reopened, the one I tried to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a note of a meeting on the 22nd of June, with General Talic. I think it should read -- is the next person there -- it's been recorded by I think Mr. Medic who made the note, as Colonel Vuketic. Should that be Vukelic or was there a Colonel Vuketic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Colonel Vukelic was present. Milutin Vukelic. This is a mistake. It's probably a typo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's been typed in the original as -- yourself, and then from the -- there were various representatives of Muslim organisations.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You yourself, I don't think, recorded this meeting in your diary, did you -- in your, I'm sorry, notebook.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an official notebook that was of small pocket format, and it remained in Banja Luka. Unfortunately, I haven't got that notebook anymore and I did record this meeting in that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you've had a chance to read through this note, even though it wasn't made by you. Was that an accurate record of the discussions that took place between General Talic and the gentlemen representing the Bosniak organisations?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a realistic portrayal. I have nothing special to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask you about one thing that was said to General Talic, in respect of Manjaca. If we look at the -- I think it's the fourth paragraph, "Gratitude was expressed to the general for enabling a visit to the captured Muslims and Croats who were in the military base at Manjaca. And General Talic was informed of some, what's called, characteristics, what the overwhelming majority were peaceful citizens who had been called to a meeting and then arrested, picked up, that they were treated extremely badly when they arrived at the camp, and that the accommodation at the camp was clearly contrary to the regulations of the Geneva Convention." Now, was that said, to your knowledge, to General Talic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended the meeting. I took part in the discussion there. Talic was told that people were arrested, even people who were beyond the age of 60, even people who had never been soldiers, intellectuals were arrested, and how should I put this, prominent figures, Croats and Bosniaks, although there were far lesser Croats. I was invited by General Talic to attend this meeting, in order for them to show to Muslim organisations that there were still active-duty officers in the army who were ethnic Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did he express any horror or surprise when this was said to him?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this information he heard from the persons who were quoted from this list, he promised that the situation would calm down, and that he was surprised, however, I mean, that Muslims had to accept this government, to go by the rules, things along those lines. However, even after this meeting, the situation was far worse than it had been before that. I have been a witness of these events, and if necessary, I can testify about that separately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I know you yourself went to Manjaca, but Colonel Selak, the Court has heard a lot of evidence and I don't think needs to hear any more about what -- I'm just concerned at the moment, please, about General Talic. Did General Talic ever, in your presence, say that he would call for an explanation from Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Popovic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Lieutenant Colonel Popovic later on he got the rank of Colonel, he issued orders on the basis of the orders he had received, and on the basis of what he thought he should do with prisoners of war -- not prisoners of war, civilian prisoners, at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now can we go, please, to the -- your notebook again for the 3rd of July?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's headed, "Kosmos maintenance and repair depot" there, and we see that General Djukic was also there, because I think you've recorded him as saying something. And then after the entry for General Djukic, you have written out, have you not, the order that we looked at earlier of the 9th of June, about instructing officers of Muslim and Croat ethnicity to take annual leave?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. The 3rd of July, I have two, Rudi Cajevec yes, Kosmos, 1030.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you find General Djukic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Djukic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then after that, have you actually written out the order of the main staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Underneath is the order of the main staff related to officers of Muslim and Croat ethnicity, that they should be sent to annual leave immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Was that the fact that it appears in your diary, in your --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the day that you were shown it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then on the -- I think that's all, in fact, that I want to ask you. If you just turn to the last page of your notebook, on this notebook.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you written, "End of active military service?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Begun on the 27th of July, 1958, ended 30th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Thank you very much, Colonel. You can put your workbook -- your official notebook away now in your briefcase. Can I ask you, please, to look at a couple more documents? First of all, disclosure 4.1605, 1st Krajina Corps, order of the 5th of July or report, rather. This is, I think, a report -- it's described as an interim report to the main staff, and states, "The head of the intelligence and security organ of the 1st Krajina Corps, Colonel Milan Stevilovic was killed in ambush organised by the Green Berets at about 1800 hours today, 5th of July, 1992." And it explains the circumstances, that it was outside Vrbanjci on the way to Kotor Varos, and his vehicle crashed into an obstacle and he was then gunned down. And with him was Stefan Markovic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. He was mutilated in the most savage manner, and as yet an unknown civilian from Kotor Varos who was in the vehicle with him was also killed. Now, the suggestion that this was a burst of enemy fire. From your knowledge, and were you still in the corps on the 5th of July, were there Muslim resistance brigades operating in Vrbanjci on the way to Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of Vrbanjci and Kotor Varos was under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps, and all communications along these lines were under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, can that be made, please, Exhibit P1589?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, next, I want you to look at, please, what we've described as the war diary of the 1st Krajina Corps, and just deal with some of the entries in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask that Ms. Gustin just brings the original so that Colonel Selak can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I read you well three days ago, because we have only got one page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's what you're going to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm going to refer to a number of pages. I'm going to put them on the ELMO and copy them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you give that to the witness, please, and then I'll give you the pages that I'm going to refer to one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you just explain to us, please, Colonel Selak, what exactly a war diary is. What was the 1st Krajina Corps obliged to do?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A war diary is an official document which all units had to keep in times of war. At the corps command, it was kept by the operative team on duty on behalf of the commander and for the commander. This is an official document about what goes on from the very beginning of war operations until their very end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, I would like you, please, first of all, just to look at a few entries which I think you can assist with. Yes. Could you please, Colonel, find -- you'll see there are some numbers at the top. Could you find a number -- an ERN number that says 01304527?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask, please, that page -- I'll give it to the usher -- page 26 and then 27, be put on. The date for this, we'd have to go back but it's the 29th of July. Do we see an entry that, "The Ozren Battalion refused to organise defence in the Dobrnja sector. They completely abandoned their positions and left for Ozren. The reason for this is the poor authority of the battalion commanders, excessive drinking and --"

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't got it -- oh, yes. "Ozren Battalion refused to organise defence in the Dobrnja region," is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And the next page, "completely abandoned their positions," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The 1st Battalion of the Prnjavor light Brigade have looted goods such as household appliances, tractors, machines, and tools and are preparing to take them home." In the event of such -- an official report of looting, what action should have been taken?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander would have had to replace this commander immediately, to take measures, disciplinary measures against him, even up to Prosecution before a court of law. Other officers subordinated to that battalion commander should be taken to task as well. Perhaps even the entire battalion would have to be replaced, dismissed from the position where they were, complete control would have to be exercised over all persons in terms of who did the looting, and disciplinary measures would have to be envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want you just, please, before we move on, to just identify the original. Is that the original?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, can you look, please, at an entry for the 1st of July? We see -- if you go to -- I think if you took the original, it's probably easier for you, Colonel, and I'm going to ask, please, that page 34 and then 35 be put up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Forget -- no, no, no, no, Colonel, when I say 34, 35 it's not you. It's the English translation so if you just find the 1st of July entry.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all if we look at our page 34, for the 1st of July, we'll see that General Talic talked to the commanders and that there was a request from General Mladic for information. And then if we put up page 35, can we see that at 1500 hours, Brdjanin came with his escort to visit the -- what's that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operative group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where would that have been?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operative group Plehan-Rabic is close to Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Would you expect a visit from the person who was in charge of the government of the region to a military post?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It's all right. Colonel, please answer the question. If you want it repeated to you, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The question is clear. The units in the front visits by representatives of the government, the political organs, the general staff, these visits were something that were necessary. The people liked that. They liked to get information. And from this diary, you can see clearly that the soldiers were satisfied, they were very happy, with Mr. Brdjanin's visit to the units in the front. This meant moral support to them, from politicians from the top authority, and who enjoyed -- who had authority, as far as the units in the front were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we look, then, please, at a couple of other entries, if the usher could give me those pages back? Could you find, please, Colonel, the entry for the 7th of July? And we'll put up page 54, please. Can you see an entry about "15 trucks were dispatched to Belgrade, eight to Belgrade and seven to Bijeljina, to pick up various goods for our unit"? It comes -- it comes under a report relating to Major Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware, because I think you were still just in the corps then, on the 7th of July, that support was being received from Belgrade for the 1st Krajina Corps's activities?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying that I personally sent columns of my vehicles with all material equipment that the units required, not only the units in -- of my corps but all the units in the area of responsibility, and this is why the -- the corridor had to function. I also sent out the salaries of the officers, the superior officers, and also to the -- to the -- my financial reports to Belgrade, and fuel and all the other things that were necessary, we received from the federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And I have that also in my official notebook, when I would send Major Pavlovic to collect the salaries from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just on that note, was your -- did you, throughout this period, and on your retirement, was your salary paid by Belgrade? Your pension as well?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All officers who were on the payroll of the Yugoslav People's Army up to the 18th of May, 1992, were on the payroll of the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I received my retirement benefits, my pension, until May 1995, until -- from Belgrade, not only I myself received it but all the other old-age pensioners too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what's going to happen. I think I'm going to take the rest of the day's session with him, so Mr. Ackerman won't have to cross-examine in which case, are we going to take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest we take a short break, if that is okay with you. We'll restrict it to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then if possible we try and finish by 1.30 or a little before, because I need to drive up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I think I'll still have the leftover of the videos for Monday morning -- Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That shouldn't present any problems to Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a short break of 15 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, can you find the entry for the 8th of July in that war diary, please, and could the usher put up page 59 and 60 on the ELMO in the translation.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you turn to the part where at 1500 hours, Colonel Ninkovic arrived?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14, just one moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he arrived for talks on further air strikes. Further air strikes on where, do you know?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strikes on the positions of the opposing side. This is probably about strikes on the Croatian side, across the Sava River, or in the defence of the towns in places where the 5th Corps was attacking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then at 1700 hours, Vojo Kupresanin, president of the autonomous region of the Bosnian Krajina arrived and discussed with General Talic the situation on the entire front.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you could turn over the page, usher, page 60, Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He underlined that the Serbian government of Bosnia-Herzegovina would do all it could to ensure that our army was organised and integrated as a unified armed force with a unified command and without paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then could you, on the same day, and could the usher put up now page 62 -- no, no, I'm sorry, it's the following day. It's the 9th of July. There is an entry that starts with the Sanski Most Battalion, commanded by Major Brajic -- I'm sorry, can we one moment go back, I'm sorry, there is one other thing I want to look at, page 61 for us. Yes, could you put up page 61 on the ELMO? I think we see that there, "a 45 vehicle convoy for Serbia was announced." Is that in the diary, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment. I haven't found that. It's in handwriting, so I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If you see --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. 9th of July, a 45-vehicle convoy for Serbia has been announced, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then going along the same entry, and if the usher could put up page 62 again, please, now. Do we see, "the Sanski Most Battalion commanded by major Brajic abandoned its position and is preparing to return home to Sanski Most with booty and the general said that Major Brajic should immediately be sent to prison, tried for failure to carry out orders and for bringing other soldiers into a hopeless situation." Do you know who Major Brajic was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Major Brajic, a Serb, I don't know where he's from, he's from Bosnia but I don't know from what town, battalion commander and he was replaced from his post. I don't know what happened to him later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we move now to the 10th of July, page 64 for us, and I'll ask that that's put up. I think it follows that -- it starts -- this entry starts with "General Mladic having called and been updated, and then the priest of Tolisa arrived in the morning to see if work had begun on refurbishing the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. church. He greeted General Talic, Colonel Simic, and Minister Martic." Do you know who is meant there by Minister Martic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minister Martic is from the Republic of the Serbian Krajina from Croatia. I never knew Mr. Martic personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then finally, on -- all I want to deal with you on this document, please, could you go to the 26th of July, please? And I'm going to put up --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry, I'm going to -- pages 123 and pages 124 of the --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- translation. This entry is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't you -- it's all right because he's not seeing this, what we are seeing on the ELMO. But I see markings on the page highlighting, and then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I have it back. It's my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then a note.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can see how I sometimes have to remind myself of the question I want to ask. Thank you. No. Sorry, 123. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The entry itself for that day is headed, "Duge Njive." That's the name of the place? I hear the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where is that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Duge Njive, I'm not sure exactly where that is. That is a forward command post of the corps. I believe that it's somewhere between Derventa -- somewhere close to Derventa but I don't know, I'm not sure. I wasn't there. It's not close to Banja Luka. It's close to Derventa, that's where Duge Njive is, but I couldn't really tell you the exact location. I know that there was a forward command post there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, we see that that day, in the morning, security was stepped up because of the consecration of a newly built church in honour of the new Serbian martyrs. No problems during the ceremony. And then we can see that General Ninkovic was there, Milan Martic, General Djukic, Arkan, and the entire ceremony was attended by the bishop of Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then next page, Mr. Usher, please, 124, just turn it over. Usher? 124, please. Oh, yes. In addition, there were the President of the Doboj municipal assembly, the chairman of the executive committee and other guests?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "And the godfather of the church was Colonel Simic and the whole consecration ceremony was filmed by Belgrade TV and there were interviews with General Talic, Colonel Simic and others. This will be historical evidence of how the Serbian army built a church during the war and handed it over to the church authorities." Two things about that. Were you aware at that stage, and had you yourself seen anywhere, the destruction that was taking place of mosques and Catholic churches in many of the municipalities in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a witness to that, unfortunately. Also in Banja Luka, all the facilities were knocked down, and also throughout Bosanska Krajina, both the Catholic and Muslim facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is vandalism which has not been seen in the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You mentioned Banja Luka. Were any mosques destroyed during 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I'm not sure. I don't think any were destroyed in 1992. I'm not sure. I cannot remember the dates but the destruction did begin. I was already retired. In the month of November, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what was the importance for all of these people, the commander of the air force, Mr. Martic from Knin or the Serbian Republic of Krajina, General Djukic, Arkan, and all the rest of them, what's the importance of all these people being seen at this ceremony?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was of major significance, because the ceremony was filmed both by TV Banja Luka and TV Belgrade. Reports were also given over the radio station and they were directed at the Serbian people and the Serbian fighters in all units of the Army of Republika Srpska, about -- and it was aimed at raising their morale. And these politicians, by their presence, made this event even more significant, both the politicians and the military leadership, and even Milan Martic came from Croatia. The Serbian people and the fighters felt that this was a significant event. Meaning that the army was helping in the construction of Orthodox religious facilities while it was destroying all the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all that I ask about this document, although tomorrow morning, when the videos -- Monday, when the videos are played, I may want to go back to just one entry. Your Honours, may I ask that the photocopy become an original, that the original -- the exhibit -- the original will be available for the Defence to have a look at if they want but it is going to be required in other trials so I don't want it to be made an exhibit here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine that is acceptable to you, Mr. Ackerman, correct. So that's how it will be, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's you very much. That's P1590.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Selak, I think -- I just want to check whether I need to put in any of -- yes, I think maybe we had better just deal with your official handover, if I can find the document. Yes. Could we have a look, please, at the report of the 14th logistics base, dated the 10th of July, 1992? The number on that is 00349346. And it's the third document -- he's already got it but it's the third document, the second page of the list. Colonel Selak, does that show the transfer of your duties between yourself and the officer who took your position, Colonel Skondric, on the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that, please, be made Exhibit 1591? I'm just wondering whether -- I don't think we need to deal with any other documents. I think it's right, as you told us, and we can see from your diary, you actually finally retired officially in September?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you -- I want to move at the end of this to deal with General Talic and Mr. Brdjanin as separate topics, but can I just ask you this: During the period of time that -- 1992, that you were in Banja Luka, did you join any kind of resistance group?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And firstly, what kind of group was it? And I'm not asking you for names or anything like that; I just want to know what sort of group it was.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a group of my colleagues, Bosniaks, who felt it was necessary to organise themselves, who wanted to see how they could help the Muslim people in Banja Luka to protect them from genocide, to survive in Banja Luka, and how we could do this. This is why we organised ourselves at that time, in mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you take any physical action to instigate any arming of any resistance groups? In other words, did you yourself procure or supply any weapons, to any group that was resisting the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single weapon, not a single bullet. We did not plan any armed action. No sabotage. We did not have any weapons. We did not give any to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've seen the size of the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka at this time. What prospect did you see of being able to mount a successful armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to mount a successful armed rebellion, one had to have well-trained men, also well-equipped with explosives and ammunition and weapons. However, I knew that the Banja Luka Corps had about 100.000 men. I knew that this was the strongest corps in the former Yugoslav People's Army, and any kind of armed action would precisely be used by the corps and the Crisis Staff for carrying out a mass genocide over the Muslim people. Mosques were mined within 15 or 20 days, in order to provoke the Muslim people to put up some kind of resistance, to engage in sabotage so that the corps and the civilian police would get a pretext for intervention and ethnic cleansing. We were precisely striving against such individual actions, and we prevented that. However, at the same time, we suggested to people to leave Banja Luka, to save their skins, because what happened in Kozarac would have been incomparably greater in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, however, that you did provide such information as you could about the events that were taking place in Banja Luka; is that correct? And in the corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The information that we obtained from the resistance staff, which I commanded, we sent this information to Sarajevo, concerning the things that were going on, the arrests of more prominent people, more educated people, among the Bosniaks, about the physical maltreatment, arrest, killing and persecution that was taking place, the activities of the Banja Luka Corps in that domain precisely, ethnic cleansing. That is the information that we sent to the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And until such time as he fled Banja Luka in 1993, were you cooperating on this aspect of information providing with Muharem Krzic, the leader of the SDA in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a brief period of time, two or three months, I provided two or three pieces of information that I had and the staff of the resistance movement, about the actions that may follow, coming from the air force, the corps units, in order to prevent a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you remained in Banja Luka until 1995. How were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed in Banja Luka until 1995, when I handed over my duty as commander of the logistics base. In mid-July, 1992, General Talic, corps commander, invited me to his office. General Ninkovic, commander of the air force of the Army of Republika Srpska, was in General Talic's office. Talic then said to me that I should not even consider moving out of Banja Luka, that I cannot leave it, and that no one would touch me. I asked him, "What do you mean nobody is going to touch me?" His answer was that the army guarantees my safety. I asked him, "What about the Red Berets and the civilian police?" His answer was, "I cannot give you any guarantees on that." I was a bit tough. I said, "Whoever may break into my apartment will be killed. I'll kill him." After that, he ordered me to return the weapons I had. I said to him that I would not carry any weapons through town. He said, "Why?" I replied that the citizens of Banja Luka do not see a balija with weapons. May I please explain this word "balija"? Balija is a derogatory term for Muslims, and that is one that was used regularly by the Serbs. The next day, a mayor -- a major and a NCO came to my apartment and they took my weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want, then, to deal, please, with some of the public statements that were made by General Talic during this period in newspapers and on television, which we'll see, and after the period, on television, for the rest of today I'd like to look at some things that were reported in newspapers. Could you now first of all be shown, please, an edition of Glas dated the 24th of April, 1992? It's disclosure 4.2168. We've got a copy here. I think we can see, can we, a photograph of General Talic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was he opening some -- some sort of exhibition or event, Western Slavonia in the whirlwind of war? And General Talic, if we look at the text, stressed the link between July 1941 and June 1991, stressing that "not even then, and certainly not now, did the people of Bosanska Krajina buckle under in front of the rampaging of fascism." Do you know, and if you don't, say so, Colonel Selak, had General Talic's family suffered during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not know. I did hear that there had been problems, but I don't have any accurate information, so I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be P1592. Now, could you be shown the next edition of Glas for the 30th of April, 1st of May, disclosure 2.107? And it's headed, "The Army Stays Here." This was a lengthy interview, we can see, with General Talic, as a result, apparently, that -- of the withdrawal of JNA units from Bosnia and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Herzegovina. There is then a description of General Talic as a child of the Krajina, and his career. And then he said this: "Write this down and underline it. Not a single bolt from a single tank of the Banja Luka Corps will leave this territory, let alone anything larger." Then a caveat that he didn't command absolutely everything. And then there were a series of questions and answers, and I don't want to go through everything. But could you find the part that's headed in the original, "A Transformation Adapted to the Region"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the reporter, apparently said to him that "The Autonomous Region of Krajina has proposed the transformation of the army into forms envisaged by the constitution of the Serbian Republic." And Talic replied, "It is no secret that there is going to be a transformation of the army. I would not like to --"

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- "talk now about what kind but I think it must be adapted to each region, that it cannot be the same all over Yugoslavia. And when this transformation comes, it is certain that the Autonomous Region of Krajina will have its share of the army." Do you remember reading this interview at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you understand he was saying when he said, "I think that the army must be adapted to each region"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He meant the Krajina Corps, the units of the Krajina Corps. He said here explicitly that a new Yugoslavia was being created, a new army, but that it will be organised according to zones within Yugoslavia. We talked about that in town. We discussed this statement of his. And it was clear to us the objective was clear, that is that they really wanted to create some new kind of Yugoslavia with these regions of Bosanska Krajina and the Krajina from Croatia, in addition to other territories. There were a lot of comments about this in town, in Banja Luka, and that is how I understood this interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we stop now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to try and finish the article, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think it will take more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You'll do me a big favour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Colonel Selak. We'll see each other again on Monday afternoon, not morning. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.24 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of January, 2003, at 2.15 p.m.
